title: Faultless Vocabulary Instruction: Guaranteeing Understanding with Structural Precision with-structural-precision
author: Jake Cowling
summary: Jake Cowling translates Engelmann and Carnine's Theory of Instruction into a concrete, five-step sequence for explicitly teaching vocabulary with precision, blended with ideas from Bringing Words to Life and The Extended Mind In Action. Working through the word "instinctively" from Matilda, he shows how to identify a concept's core, invariant meaning while separating out the irrelevant contextual features that must be varied across examples; present multiple positive examples that keep the critical attributes constant while varying everything else; introduce negative examples via minimal difference and immediate juxtaposition to sharpen the boundary; test generalisation by having students label new, unlabelled examples and articulate why using a sentence frame; and only then connect the taught concept back to its original appearance in the source text. His central argument, following Engelmann, is that most teaching failures are actually instructional failures -- communication failures caused by examples whose structural features allow misinterpretation -- not student failures.
points: Cowling's reframing of teaching failure as instructional failure -- caused by examples that structurally allow misinterpretation or misgeneralisation -- shifts responsibility from "the student didn't get it" to "the examples weren't precise enough."

His five-step sequence (identify core meaning, establish positive boundary, establish negative boundary via minimal difference, test generalisation, connect back to source) gives teachers a reusable template for any piece of explicit vocabulary instruction, not just the worked "instinctively" example.

The minimal-difference and immediate-juxtaposition technique for negative examples is the piece's sharpest mechanism: presenting a positive and contrasting negative example back-to-back forces attention onto the exact feature that flips the word's applicability.

Cowling's closing step -- deliberately not defining the word using the word itself, and only returning to the original text passage after the concept is secure -- inverts the common practice of starting vocabulary instruction with the text.
quotes: Teaching failures often aren’t student failures, they are instructional failures, which are fundamentally communication failures.
Instruction is faulty when the structural features of the examples allow for misinterpretation or misgeneralisation by the learner.
Keep your teacher wording identical each time. This constant signal highlights the constant feature (the sameness) across all the changing contexts (irrelevant variation).
To establish the rule, we must use juxtaposition: present the positive and its contrasting negative example immediately together. This focuses the learner’s attention on the flipping feature.
If your instruction was faultless, the learner will be able to generalise the concept by correctly applying the label to new, unlabelled examples.
This approach moves vocabulary teaching from tell and hope to structural design and guaranteed comprehension.
